a: On the third day
p: The last day of Esther's fast (4:16). Jews and Christians noticed how often rescue comes on a third day.
b: Esther had asked the Jews of Susa to fast for her: "For three days, night and day, eat nothing and drink nothing" (4:16), so this is the last day of the fast, and she goes in hungry. The rabbis gathered verses in which something decisive happens "on the third day": Abraham sees the mountain of the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:4), Israel meets God at Sinai (Exodus 19:16), and Hosea promises that God will raise his people up on the third day (Hosea 6:2). Genesis Rabbah 56:1 puts Esther 5:1 in that list. Christian readers have heard the same pattern in Jesus' rising on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:4). The text itself makes no such link; it only counts the days of the fast.

a: Esther dressed herself as queen
p: The Hebrew has no word for clothes here. It says Esther "put on royalty."
b: The phrase is vattilbash Ester malkhut, "Esther put on royalty." Most translations supply "robes" or "clothes," since the word malkhut elsewhere in the book means "kingdom" or "royal" and is used with clothing in 6:8 and 8:15. The short form may be deliberate: the young woman who hid who she was (2:10) now takes on the role of queen in full. The Talmud reads the odd wording as a hint: "It does not say royal clothes, but royalty: the holy spirit clothed her" (Bavli Megillah 14b). The Plain keeps the sense of the Hebrew without adding a noun it does not have.
orig: וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת (vattilbash Ester malkhut), 'Esther put on royalty'

a: The king was sitting on his royal throne inside the royal hall, across from the doorway of the building
p: The throne faced the doorway, so the king could see across the inner court. On Susa's palace, see the note on 1:2.
b: On Susa and the palace that Darius I built there, see the note on 1:2; on the reliefs of an enthroned king receiving visitors, see the note on 4:11. The point here is the layout. The king sits facing the doorway, so that anyone standing in the inner court is seen at once. Esther cannot wait unseen for a good moment: as soon as she takes her place, the king's decision is in front of her. How the courts and halls named in Esther fit the excavated buildings is uncertain.

a: the gold scepter that was in his hand
t: The scepter and the rule of 4:11
p: The scepter held out meant life for someone who had come in uncalled (4:11). Esther touches its tip.
b: Esther had told Mordecai that anyone who came to the king uncalled would die, unless the king held out the gold scepter (4:11; see the note there on the guarded Persian court). Now the king does it, and she touches the top of the scepter, accepting his grace. The Hebrew tells the moment in two calm sentences and gives no reason for the king's favor beyond the fact that "she gained his favor," the same phrase used when she first won him in 2:17. The Greek here adds a long scene in which she faints and God changes the king's heart (see the variants on 5:1 and 5:2).

a: Even if it is half the kingdom
p: A royal way of saying "anything you like." Herod uses the same words to Herodias' daughter in Mark 6:23.
b: The phrase is a courtly overstatement, not a real offer to divide the empire; the king repeats it in 5:6, 7:2 and, in a shorter form, 9:12. In the Gospel of Mark, Herod Antipas makes the same promise to the dancing daughter of Herodias, and her request is John the Baptist's head (Mark 6:23). Herodotus tells a story about Xerxes himself that shows the danger of such promises: he swore to give a woman of his court whatever she asked, and she asked for the robe his wife Amestris had woven for him (Herodotus, Histories 9.109–111). Esther, by contrast, does not ask yet.

a: let the king come today with Haman
t: God's name in the first letters?
p: In Hebrew, the first letters of four words here spell YHWH. Jewish tradition noticed it, but it is probably chance.
b: The Hebrew words yavo hammelekh vehaman hayyom, "let come the king and Haman today," begin with the letters Y, H, W, H, the four letters of God's name, YHWH. Medieval scribes sometimes wrote those letters larger, and Jewish tradition pointed to three more such patterns (1:20; 5:13; 7:7), finding God hidden in a book that never names him. Most modern scholars treat the patterns as accidental: in a long Hebrew text such strings of letters turn up by chance, and the others need reading backward or using last letters. The claim is old and widely repeated, but it does not show in any translation and is not something the text points to.
orig: יָבוֹא הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהָמָן הַיּוֹם (yavo hammelekh vehaman hayyom)

a: to the feast that I have made for him
p: Esther invites her enemy to dinner. The Talmud lists twelve guesses at her reasons.
b: The narrator never says why Esther delays or why she brings Haman. The rabbis offered many reasons: to lull Haman into feeling safe; to make the king jealous of him; so that the Jews would not lean on her but keep praying; to catch Haman off guard; to keep him close so he could not plot (Bavli Megillah 15b lists twelve). Modern readers see good court strategy: she makes the king curious, builds up his promise in public, and gets Haman into a room where she controls the moment (Fox; Berlin). Some also note the delay lets the events of chapter 6 happen first. The Plain keeps her reason hidden, as the text does.

a: At the wine feast
p: The "wine feast" was the drinking after the meal. Greek writers said Persians decided serious matters while drinking.
b: The phrase mishteh hayyayin, "feast of wine," means the drinking that followed the meal (also 7:2, 7–8). Herodotus reports that the Persians liked to debate important matters while drunk, and then to look at the decision again sober the next day, or the other way around (Herodotus, Histories 1.133). Whether or not that is exact, the book shows a court where wine and decisions go together: Vashti is summoned while the king is merry with wine (1:10), and the decree against the Jews is followed by the king and Haman sitting down to drink (3:15). Esther now uses the same setting.

a: Then tomorrow I will do what the king asks of me
p: Esther starts to make her request in 5:7, then asks for another feast. Hesitation, or strategy?
b: Verse 7 begins "Here is what I ask, and what I want," and then she asks only for another feast. Some readers think her nerve fails at the last moment. Others think she is pressing her advantage: by saying "tomorrow I will do what the king asks," she turns her request into a favor the king has asked of her, and he has now promised twice, in front of Haman, to grant it (Fox, Bush). The rabbis said she delayed so that Haman's pride would grow (Bavli Megillah 15b). Either way, the night between the two feasts is when everything changes (6:1).

a: Mordecai did not get up, and did not shake with fear in front of him
t: He would not stand or tremble
p: Mordecai had already refused to bow (3:2). Now he will not even rise, though he has just ended a three-day fast.
b: The verb za', "tremble, shake," is rare (it is used of the house's guards trembling in Ecclesiastes 12:3). Mordecai's refusal goes back to 3:2–5, where he will not bow down to Haman; why he refused is discussed there. Here the stakes are higher: Haman's decree has gone out, and Mordecai has been in sackcloth (4:1). He still gives Haman no sign of respect or fear. The scene sets Haman's mood swing: he leaves the queen's feast happy and is filled with rage at one man sitting in the gate.
orig: וְלֹא־קָם וְלֹא־זָע מִמֶּנּוּ (velo qam velo za' mimmennu)

a: But Haman kept control of himself
p: The same Hebrew verb describes Joseph holding back his tears. Esther borrows much from the Joseph story.
b: The verb hit'appaq, "control oneself, hold back," is used of Joseph when he sees his brothers: "he washed his face, came out, and controlled himself" (Genesis 43:31), and later when he "could no longer hold himself back" (Genesis 45:1). Saul uses it at Gilgal: "So I pushed myself to do it, and I offered the burnt offering" (1 Samuel 13:12). Scholars have long noted that Esther echoes the Joseph story: a Jew rises at a foreign court, a signet ring is handed over, and a man is paraded in royal clothes (see the notes on 6:9 and 8:2). Haman, though, holds back only to plot.

a: the number of his sons
p: Herodotus says Persians prized many sons next to courage, and the king rewarded the man with the most.
b: Herodotus writes that, after valor in battle, the Persians thought it the finest thing to have many sons, and that each year the king sent gifts to the man who had the most (Herodotus, Histories 1.136). Haman's boast fits that world. The reader will learn in 9:7–10 that he has ten sons, and that they will all die. His list moves from wealth to sons to the king's favor, and he will lose all three: his house goes to Esther (8:1), his sons are killed (9:10), and the king's favor turns to Mordecai (8:2).

a: Yet all this is not enough for me
p: Haman has wealth, sons and the king's favor, but one man's refusal to stand spoils it all for him.
b: The book draws Haman as a study in wounded pride: everything he has "is not enough" (enennu shoveh li, literally "is not worth it to me") while one Jew will not honor him. Jewish moral teaching has often used him as the type of the envious man whom no success satisfies, and Christian preachers have read him alongside the warning that pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18). Fox notes that Haman's self-love is also his weakness: it is exactly what makes him misread the king's question in 6:6. Some find another hidden divine name in the last letters of this phrase in Hebrew (see the note on 5:4).

a: a pole fifty cubits tall
p: A pole about 75 feet high: far taller than needed, so that all Susa would see it.
b: On the pole itself (Hebrew 'ets, "tree, pole"), and on impaling and the display of bodies in Persia, see the note on 2:23. Fifty cubits is about 75 feet (23 meters), the height of a seven-story building. No one needs a pole that tall to kill a man. The size shows Haman's hatred to the whole city and his wish to make Mordecai's death a public lesson, and many readers hear in it the story's dark humor: the bigger the pole, the more public Haman's own end will be (7:9). The Greek calls it a xylon, "wood." Rabbinic tradition, taking the number literally, asked where Haman found such a tree.
orig: עֵץ גָּבֹהַּ חֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה ('ets gavoah chamishim ammah), 'a tree, high, fifty cubits'

a: That night sleep ran away from the king
p: The book never names God, but its turning point is a king who cannot sleep. Readers have argued over what that means.
b: Many scholars see this verse as the hinge of the whole book: from here every plot of Haman's falls back on him (Berg, Levenson). The Hebrew simply says the king's sleep "fled." The Greek Septuagint names the cause: "the Lord took the sleep away from the king" (see the variant). The Talmud reads "the king" here as the King of the universe: "the sleep of the King of the world fled," since God was stirred to act (Bavli Megillah 15b). Esther Rabbah 10:1 sets this night beside Psalm 121:4, where the Keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, and Psalm 44:23, which asks the Lord why he sleeps. Christian readers have taken the verse as a classic picture of providence, God working through ordinary events without being seen. Critical readers point out that the book leaves the cause open on purpose, and that a reader may see chance, or more than chance. The narrator never decides for us.
r: 4:14; 6:13; Genesis 41:1; Daniel 2:1; Daniel 6:18; Proverbs 21:1; Psalm 121:4; Psalm 44:23

a: the book of remembrances, the daily records
p: The Hebrew calls the record "the book of remembrances," a phrase that recalls God's own book of remembrance in Malachi 3:16.
b: In 2:23 the record was called "the book of the daily records"; here it is sefer hazzikhronot divre hayyamim, "the book of remembrances, the daily records" (on Persian record-keeping, see the note on 2:23). The word "remembrances" (zikhronot) recalls Malachi's "book of remembrance" written before the LORD for those who fear him (Malachi 3:16), and the scroll in which Moses was told to write the memory of Amalek's defeat (Exodus 17:14). Esther ends with remembrance too: the days of Purim are "to be remembered" (9:28). The king's book remembers what the king forgot; readers who see God's hand in the book find a quiet hint here that another record is being kept.

a: Bigthana
p: In 2:21 the same eunuch is called Bigthan. The extra letter is a spelling variation, not a different man.
b: The Hebrew spells the name Bigthan in 2:21 and Bigthana here; the Greek Septuagint at this point simply says "the two eunuchs." Persian names in Esther often vary in spelling, and copyists were less fixed with foreign names. The name may be Persian Bagadana, "gift of God" (a known Old Persian type of name), but that is a guess. The plot itself is told in 2:21–23.

a: What honor and what high rank was given to Mordecai for this?
p: Persian kings were known for rewarding those who saved or served them. Mordecai had been left out.
b: Greek sources picture Persian kings as eager to repay a good deed, since a king's generosity proved his power. A letter of Xerxes quoted by Thucydides tells the Spartan Pausanias that his service "is laid up in our house, recorded forever" (Thucydides, History 1.129). Herodotus tells of Syloson, who once gave Darius a cloak and later received the island of Samos as his reward (Herodotus, Histories 3.139–141). That makes the answer "Not a thing has been done for him" a small scandal at court: Mordecai saved the king's life and got nothing. The delay, from 2:23 to this night, is what makes the timing so sharp.

a: Haman had just come into the palace's outer court
p: While the king is looking for a way to honor Mordecai, Haman arrives early to ask for Mordecai's death.
b: The narrator lays the two plans side by side. The king wants to reward Mordecai; Haman has come so early that he is already in the outer court, ready to ask permission to hang Mordecai on the pole he built in the night (5:14). He never gets to say it. Fox and others see the scene as the book's finest piece of irony: Haman is in the right place at the right time, and that is his undoing. Readers who see God's hand in the book point to the timing as one of its quiet signs.

a: the man the king takes pleasure in honoring
p: The full phrase comes five times in the chapter. Haman hears it once and assumes it means himself.
b: The Hebrew ha'ish asher hammelekh chafets biqaro, "the man whom the king delights in his honor," comes five times: the king asks it (6:6), Haman repeats it in his answer (6:7), uses it twice in his plan, once for dressing the man and once in the herald's cry (6:9), and then must shout it himself in the square (6:11). Haman's own thought in 6:6 uses a shorter form of the same words. The Plain keeps the same English each time so the reader can hear the repetition grow heavier. The narrator lets us into Haman's thoughts ("Haman told himself"), a rare move in Hebrew narrative, so that the reader knows the joke before Haman does.
orig: הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר הַמֶּלֶךְ חָפֵץ בִּיקָרוֹ (ha'ish asher hammelekh chafets biqaro)

a: whose head has been decked with a royal crown
p: The Hebrew most naturally puts the crown on the horse's head, not the man's. The king leaves the crown out in 6:10.
b: The words "on its head" (berosho) could refer to the horse or to the king. The grammar favors the horse: Assyrian and Persian reliefs show royal horses with a tall ornament between the ears. The KJV took it as the king's own crown ("the crown royal which is set upon his head"), and some modern readers agree. Either way Haman is asking for the king's own things: his clothes, his horse, his crown. In his reply (6:10) the king names only the clothes and the horse; whether he drops the crown on purpose is not said, but many readers see Haman's request as reaching too far toward the throne.
orig: וַאֲשֶׁר נִתַּן כֶּתֶר מַלְכוּת בְּרֹאשׁוֹ (va'asher nittan keter malkhut berosho)

a: lead him through the open square of the city
p: Royal clothes, the king's horse, and a herald calling out ahead: the scene follows Joseph's honor in Egypt.
b: Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring and fine clothes, "had him ride in his second chariot, and they shouted ahead of him, 'Abrek!'" (Genesis 41:43). Mordecai is dressed in royal clothes and led on the king's horse with a herald calling ahead (6:11), and he will also get the signet ring (8:2) and become second to the king (10:3). Solomon too was set on King David's own mule to show he was the chosen heir (1 Kings 1:33). The parallels support the view that Esther was written with the Joseph story in mind, as a story of a Jew who rises in a foreign court to save his people.

a: he had covered his head
p: Covering the head was a sign of mourning or shame, as when David fled from Absalom.
b: When David fled Jerusalem, "his head was covered, and he walked barefoot" (2 Samuel 15:30); Jeremiah describes farmers who "cover their heads" in shame during a drought (Jeremiah 14:3–4). Haman goes home in the posture of a mourner, the way Mordecai went about in sackcloth in 4:1. A Talmudic story adds that as Haman led Mordecai through the streets, his own daughter, thinking the man on the horse was her father, emptied a chamber pot on the walker's head, and then threw herself from the roof (Bavli Megillah 16a). The Hebrew text says only that he hurried home with his head covered. Compare 7:8, where Haman's face is covered again.

a: his wise men
p: Haman's friends are now called his "wise men," the same title as the king's advisers in 1:13.
b: In 5:10 and 5:14 they were simply "his friends." Now the narrator calls them chakhamav, "his wise men," the word used for the king's experts "skilled in reading the times" in 1:13. Some read the shift as irony: Haman's "wise men" can see the end only after it is already coming. Others think they are named as such because they now speak like seers, predicting his fall. Zeresh, who proposed the pole in 5:14, now speaks again with them.

a: If he comes from the Jewish people, you will not get the better of him
t: "You will not get the better of him"
p: Haman's own household predicts his fall because Mordecai is a Jew. The Greek adds "because the living God is with him."
b: Why would a Persian's advisers say this? The text does not explain, but readers have offered answers. The Greek makes it explicit: "because the living God is with him" (see the variant). The Talmud has Haman's advisers compare the Jews to dust and stars: when they go down, they go all the way down, and when they rise, they rise to the stars (Bavli Megillah 16a). Many see an echo of Amalek's old defeat by Israel (Exodus 17:8–16), since Haman is an Agagite (3:1). Others compare foreigners in the Bible who see that Israel's God fights for them, like Rahab (Joshua 2:9) and Balaam (Numbers 23–24). The phrase "from the Jewish people" is literally "from the seed of the Jews," an unusual way of putting it.

a: My people are what I want
p: For the first time Esther says out loud to the king that she belongs to the people Haman wants destroyed.
b: At first Esther "did not let anyone know which people or family she came from" (2:10; compare 2:20). Now she pairs her own life with her people's: "my life is what I ask... my people are what I want." She does not yet use the word "Jews"; she lets the king discover that the decree he signed touches his own queen. Many readers see here the book's answer to Mordecai's warning that she would not escape just because she was in the palace (4:13–14). For Jews living among the nations, Esther's choice to stand with her people when hiding was possible became a model of courage and solidarity.

a: sold as slaves, men and women
t: Sold as slaves, men and women
p: Esther's words echo the last curse of Deuteronomy 28, where Israel tries to sell itself as slaves and no one will buy.
b: "We have been sold" recalls the silver Haman offered for the Jews (3:9; 4:7). The pair la'avadim velishfachot, "as male slaves and female slaves," also matches the last of the covenant curses: "There you will try to sell yourselves to your enemies as slaves, men and women, and no one will want to buy you" (Deuteronomy 28:68). Esther says that even slavery, the worst fate Moses named, she could have borne in silence; Haman's decree is worse. Whether the author meant the echo is debated, but it fits a book for Jews still living among the nations, far from the land, under the shadow of Deuteronomy's warnings.

a: That trouble would not have been worth bothering the king.
p: Unclear Hebrew: "the trouble is not worth bothering the king," or "the enemy cannot repay the king's loss."
b: The words ki ein hatsar shoveh benezeq hammelekh have three common readings. (1) Tsar as "trouble": slavery would be a hardship not worth the king's being troubled about, so Esther would have kept quiet (Moore, Fox, Bush; the Plain). (2) Tsar as "enemy": "the enemy could not make up for the king's loss," since a destroyed people pays no taxes (KJV "the enemy could not countervail the king's damage"; Rashi). The same word means "adversary" two verses later (7:6), which supports this reading. (3) The Greek has a different line: "for the slanderer is not worthy of the king's court" (see the variant). Nezeq, "loss, damage, bother," is an Aramaic-type word used only here in the Hebrew Bible.
orig: כִּי אֵין הַצָּר שֹׁוֶה בְּנֵזֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ (ki ein hatsar shoveh benezeq hammelekh)

a: King Ahasuerus spoke. He said to Queen Esther
p: The Hebrew says the king "said" twice. It may show his shock, or it may be a scribal doubling.
b: The Hebrew reads vayyomer hammelekh Achashverosh vayyomer le'Ester hammalkah, "King Ahasuerus said, and he said to Queen Esther." Some take the doubling as a picture of the king stammering in shock. The Talmud explains that until now he had spoken to her through an interpreter, but when he learned she was of royal descent (from Saul's line) he spoke to her directly (Bavli Megillah 16a). Others think a scribe wrote the verb twice by mistake. The Plain keeps two verbs with a short pause. His questions, "Who is this man, and where is he?" show that he does not connect the decree he sealed (3:10–11) with the people he is now told are hers.
orig: וַיֹּאמֶר הַמֶּלֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ וַיֹּאמֶר לְאֶסְתֵּר הַמַּלְכָּה

a: The adversary, the enemy, is this evil man, Haman!
p: Esther names Haman and leaves the king out, though the king had approved the decree.
b: The king had handed Haman his ring and the Jews' lives (3:10–11), but Esther blames only Haman: "adversary" (tsar) and "enemy" (oyev), and "evil." Most readers see wise tact: a queen cannot accuse the king to his face, and by casting Haman as the king's enemy too (he was ready to destroy the queen and the man who saved the king's life) she makes the king's anger work for her (Fox, Berlin). Some ethical readers wish she had named the king's part. The book seems more interested in how a Jew in a foreign court survives than in calling the king to account.

a: the king had settled on doing him harm
p: The same Hebrew describes Saul's settled plan to kill David (1 Samuel 20:33).
b: The Hebrew ki khaletah elav hara'ah me'et hammelekh, literally "that harm was finished against him from the king," uses an idiom found in 1 Samuel 20, where Jonathan tests whether Saul "has settled on doing evil" (1 Samuel 20:7) and learns that "his father had settled on killing David" (1 Samuel 20:33). Since Mordecai is of the family of Saul's father Kish (2:5) and Haman is an Agagite (3:1), the echo of Saul's story may be meant. Jewish tradition also found a hidden divine name in the final letters of four words here (see the note on 5:4).

a: went out to the palace garden
p: The king leaves in a rage. He may be angry at Haman, or caught between his queen and the decree he himself sealed.
b: The palace garden is the same garden court where the book opened with a royal feast (1:5); Persian kings were famous for their walled gardens, the paradeisoi, the word that gives us "paradise." The text gives no reason for the king's exit. Many readers think he needed time: he had sealed the decree himself (3:10–12), and a Persian law could not be undone (8:8). Others see a man who cannot think except when his anger tells him what to do. Haman uses the moment badly, staying with the queen when the king's honor is at stake.

a: Haman had fallen across the couch Esther was on
p: Haman throws himself on the queen's couch to beg, and the king sees an assault. His wife's warning comes true.
b: At Persian feasts guests reclined on couches (compare 1:6). Greek writers report that the harem was strictly guarded and that men were forbidden to approach the king's women (Plutarch, Artaxerxes 27). Haman, begging for his life, "had fallen" (nofel) on the queen's couch, the same verb his advisers used: "you are sure to fall before him" (6:13). The Talmud says an angel pushed him (Bavli Megillah 16a). The king's charge is almost certainly unfair, and the narrator knows it. Some readers note that Esther does nothing to correct him. The book lets Haman be condemned for the wrong crime and leaves the reader to judge.

a: Would he even force himself on the queen
p: The verb kavash means to subdue or conquer. Used of a woman it means to overpower her.
b: Kavash is the verb of Genesis 1:28 ("subdue the earth") and of conquering land (Numbers 32:22); Nehemiah uses it of Israelite daughters forced into slavery (Nehemiah 5:5). The Greek renders it biazē, "use force on." The king's words turn a desperate plea into a capital crime against the king's own house.
orig: הֲגַם לִכְבּוֹשׁ אֶת־הַמַּלְכָּה (hagam likhbosh et hammalkah)

a: Haman's face was covered
p: Covering the face of a condemned man was a sign of death. The Greek reads "his face changed."
b: No one gives an order; Haman's face is simply covered, and he is as good as dead. A close parallel comes from early Rome, where the formula for executing a traitor was "cover his head, hang him on the barren tree" (Livy, History of Rome 1.26). Greek and Roman writers also tell of the condemned having their heads covered. Some scholars, finding no Persian evidence, have suggested a small change to the Hebrew so that it reads "Haman's face turned pale" or "flushed," and the Greek has "Haman's face was changed" (see the variant). The Plain follows the Hebrew. Compare 6:12, where Haman covered his own head.

a: Harbona, one of the eunuchs who stood before the king
p: Harbona was one of the seven eunuchs sent for Vashti (1:10). Purim songs still bless his name.
b: Harbona appears first among the eunuchs sent to fetch Vashti (1:10). Here he speaks at exactly the right moment and points out the pole. The saying "Harbona, remembered for good" is already found in the Jerusalem Talmud (Yerushalmi Megillah 3:7), and the Purim hymn Shoshanat Ya'akov, sung after the reading of the Megillah, ends with it. Rabbi Eleazar said in the Babylonian Talmud that Harbona had been part of Haman's plot and switched sides when he saw it failing (Bavli Megillah 16a). Esther Rabbah says instead that the prophet Elijah appeared in Harbona's form (Esther Rabbah 10:9). The text itself shows only a palace servant who knows where the pole is and why it was built. The Greek names him Bougathan, the Alpha Text Agathas (see the variant).

a: the man whose words did the king good
p: Harbona reminds the king that the pole was meant for the man who had saved his life.
b: Literally "Mordecai, who spoke good for the king," pointing back to 2:22 and to the reading of the records in 6:2. Harbona's words turn Haman's plot into a crime against the king: he planned to kill the king's benefactor. The king needs no more. In Hebrew the king's sentence is two words, tluhu alav, "hang him on it."
orig: אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר־טוֹב עַל־הַמֶּלֶךְ (asher dibber tov 'al hammelekh)

a: So they hanged Haman on the pole he had readied for Mordecai
p: The plot falls back on the plotter. The Psalms and Proverbs say the same of the one who digs a pit.
b: This is the book's most famous reversal, and Mordecai's letter will sum it up: Haman's evil plot came back "on his own head" (9:25). The Bible often says that the wicked fall into what they prepare for others. A psalm of David says that the one who digs a pit falls into the hole he made, and his violence comes down on his own head (Psalm 7:15–16); a proverb says that whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone rolled will roll back on the one who rolls it (Proverbs 26:27). Daniel's accusers are thrown to the lions they meant for him (Daniel 6:24). Psalms, Proverbs and Daniel are not yet translated on this site, so they are described here, not quoted.
r: 9:25; Psalm 7:15–16; Psalm 9:15–16; Proverbs 26:27; Proverbs 11:8; Ecclesiastes 10:8; Daniel 6:24

a: the king calmed down from his rage
p: The same verb ended the Vashti story in 2:1. One queen fell when it cooled; now an enemy has.
b: The Hebrew verb shakhakh, "cool, subside," is used of the king's anger only here and in 2:1, where "King Ahasuerus calmed down from his anger" and then thought of Vashti. The Plain uses the same English for both. The two stories are framed alike: the king's anger is roused by a breach of honor at a feast, someone is removed, and the anger cools. This time the one removed is Haman.

a: the house of Haman
p: In the ancient Near East the property of a man executed for treason went to the crown. The king gives it to Esther.
b: "House" means Haman's whole estate: his property, his household and probably his servants. Persian kings took the goods of condemned men: Herodotus tells how Darius had the rebel governor Oroetes killed and his wealth brought to Susa (Herodotus, Histories 3.128–129), and Ezra's decree threatens that a lawbreaker's house will be torn down (Ezra 6:11). The king hands the house to Esther, and she puts Mordecai over it (8:2). Haman had boasted of his riches (5:11); now they belong to the people he meant to plunder (3:13).

a: The king slipped off the signet ring he had taken back from Haman
p: The ring the king gave Haman in 3:10 now goes to Mordecai, as Pharaoh's ring went to Joseph.
b: The same Hebrew verb opened 3:10, when the king "slipped the signet ring off his hand" and gave it to Haman (see the note there, with the Joseph parallel in Genesis 41:42). A Persian king's seal made a document law (8:8), and thousands of seal impressions survive on clay tablets from Persepolis. Now the power to write in the king's name belongs to Mordecai. Haman's ring, his house and his place all pass to the man he wanted dead, and Esther, not the king, sets Mordecai over Haman's house.

a: She threw herself down at his feet in tears
p: Haman is dead, but his decree is still law. Esther has to go to the king a second time.
b: Haman's death has saved Esther and Mordecai, but the letters sealed with the king's ring still order the death of every Jew on the 13th of Adar (3:13). So Esther comes again, apparently unbidden, and the king again holds out the scepter (8:4; compare 4:11 and 5:2). This time she weeps and falls at his feet, which some find a step back from the commanding queen of chapter 7. Others see the right posture for a petition against a royal decree: she asks for mercy, not justice, and lets the king find the way (Fox; Day). Her plea is for her people, not herself; in 8:5 she speaks to the king of "the Jews" for the first time.

a: to turn back the letters
p: Esther asks the king to reverse the letters, and she calls them Haman's plot, not the king's decree.
b: The verb lehashiv means "to bring back, reverse." The same root returns in 8:8 (no royal document can be "turned back") and in 9:25, where Haman's plot "must come back" (yashuv) on his own head. Esther piles up four polite conditions, more than anywhere else in the book, and she calls the letters "the plot of Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite," though they went out in the king's name with his seal (3:12). The king's answer shows that her request cannot be granted as asked (8:8).

a: my kin
p: Esther now names what she once hid: "which people or family she came from" (2:10).
b: The word moladti, "my kindred, my birth family," is the same word used in 2:10, where Esther "did not let anyone know which people or family she came from." Her two questions turn that silence around. They echo Judah's plea to Joseph in Joseph's house in Egypt: "How could I go up to my father without the boy beside me? I could not bear to watch the grief that would overtake my father" (Genesis 44:34). The Hebrew shares more than the plea: Esther's "the evil that will find my people" (bara'ah asher yimtsa) uses the same words as Judah's "the grief (evil) that would find my father." In both speeches someone close to a foreign ruler pleads for their family by saying they cannot bear to see them harmed.

a: no one can turn back
t: What the king can and cannot do
p: The king cannot cancel Haman's letters, but he can let Esther and Mordecai write another letter with the same authority.
b: On the rule that a sealed Persian law could not be revoked, see the note on 1:19. The king's answer explains the shape of the rest of the book. He cannot do what Esther asked (8:5), but he gives Esther and Mordecai the same power he gave Haman: to write "whatever seems good to you" in his name and seal it with his ring (compare 3:11). The answer to one decree has to be another. The king's own words, "What is written in the king's name... no one can turn back," now protect Mordecai's letter as well, since it too will be sealed with the king's ring.

a: It was the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan
p: Sivan is late spring (May–June). The counter-letter goes out about seventy days after Haman's letter.
b: Haman's letters were written on the 13th of the first month, Nisan (3:12). This letter is dated the 23rd of Sivan, about seventy days later, leaving almost nine months before the 13th of Adar. The month names are Babylonian (Nisanu, Simanu, Addaru), which Jews took up after the exile (compare Nehemiah 1:1; Nehemiah 2:1; Zechariah 1:7). The Greek moves the date to the first month, Nisan (see the variant). This verse, with 43 Hebrew words, is often said to be the longest verse in the Hebrew Bible; the Plain breaks it into short sentences.

a: and to the Jews in their writing and their tongue
p: Haman's decree was sent about the Jews; this one is sent to them, in their own writing and language.
b: The list copies 3:12 almost word for word, with two changes: the letter goes first "to the Jews," and a closing phrase adds "to the Jews in their writing and their tongue." The Plain uses the same wording as 1:22 and 3:12 where the Hebrew is the same. The Jews are no longer the object of a decree but a people addressed by the empire. Which language is meant is not said: Hebrew, or Aramaic, the language most Jews of the Persian period used in daily life (Nehemiah complains of children who "could not speak Judean," Nehemiah 13:24). For a scattered people this mattered: the empire's law came to them as one people, in their own words.

a: They rode fast steeds that served the crown, foals of the mares
p: Two rare Persian words describe the horses. The KJV, guessing, made them "mules, camels, and young dromedaries."
b: The Hebrew is rokhvei harekhesh ha'achashteranim bene haramakhim, "riders of the steeds, the royal ones, sons of the mares." Rekhesh means swift horses (1 Kings 4:28; Micah 1:13). Achashteranim is a loanword, probably from Old Persian khshathra, "rule, kingdom," so "royal" or "of the crown's service." Ramakhim is thought to mean mares, though that too is uncertain. The KJV's "riders on mules, camels, and young dromedaries" followed medieval guesses and is almost certainly wrong. The point is speed: the best horses of the royal post (see the note on 3:13) were sent so that Mordecai's letter could catch up with Haman's.

a: little children and women
p: The words copy 3:13. They may permit killing attackers' families, or describe attacks on Jewish families.
b: The Hebrew follows 3:13 word for word, turned around: "annihilate, kill and destroy... little children and women," and property "taken as plunder." Most translators read it as permission for the Jews to do to their attackers what Haman had permitted against them, families included (KJV and most modern versions; Fox, Moore). Robert Gordis argued that "little children and women" belongs with "them": the Jews may destroy any force "that comes against them, their little children and women," so the verse speaks of defending Jewish families (Gordis 1976; some recent versions follow him). Either way, when the fighting comes, the text counts only "men" killed (9:6, 15) and says three times that the Jews did not take plunder (9:10, 15, 16). The Plain keeps the Hebrew's word order, with no added "with" or "their," so the ambiguity stays.

a: stand up for their lives
p: The phrase means self-defense: to stand one's ground to save one's life.
b: La'amod 'al nafsham, literally "to stand over their life," is used again in 9:16. The decree does not let the Jews attack whom they like; it lets them gather and defend themselves against "any people or province that comes against them." In 9:2 they act against those "looking to do them harm." How far the actual fighting stayed within those limits is debated (see the notes on 9:5 and 9:13).

a: to get vengeance from their enemies
p: The verb naqam often means rightful punishment by a lawful authority, not private revenge.
b: Lehinnaqem is the reflexive form, "to avenge themselves." In the Hebrew Bible naqam is often the act of a legitimate power putting wrong right: God's vengeance (Deuteronomy 32:35, 43), or a king's, as when Saul asks for Philistine foreskins "to get revenge on the king's enemies" (1 Samuel 18:25). George Mendenhall argued that it usually means lawful vindication, not a blood feud, and many commentators read it that way here: the Jews act under the king's law against those who would carry out Haman's (Mendenhall; Bush). Others take it more plainly as revenge and are troubled by it. The Hebrew writes the word "ready" in two spellings, atidim read and atudim written, with the same meaning.

a: royal clothes of blue-violet and white
p: Mordecai wears the palace colors of 1:6. He went out in sackcloth in 4:1; now he wears royal clothes.
b: Blue-violet (tekhelet) and white were the colors of the hangings at the king's feast (1:6), and purple and fine linen mark wealth and rank (compare Daniel 5:29; Luke 16:19). Xenophon describes the Persian king's purple tunic with white in it (Cyropaedia 8.3.13). The "crown" here is an 'atarah, a wreath or headband, not the king's keter. The change of clothes caps a pattern: Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth (4:1), refused the clothes Esther sent (4:4), was dressed in the king's clothes for a day (6:11), and now wears royal clothes of his own.

a: The city of Susa cheered and was glad
p: When Haman's decree went out, the city of Susa was "in turmoil" (3:15). Now it cheers.
b: The book sets the two scenes side by side: after the first decree "the king and Haman sat down to drink, while the city of Susa was in turmoil" (3:15); after the second, Mordecai walks out in royal clothes and the city rejoices. A proverb puts the same thought in general terms: when the righteous do well, a city is glad (Proverbs 11:10). The book implies that Haman's policy was never popular even among non-Jews in the capital.

a: For the Jews there was light and joy, gladness and honor.
p: This verse is said every Saturday night in the Havdalah service, with the prayer "so may it be for us."
b: "Light" here means good fortune, as in "Light is scattered like seed for the righteous" (Psalm 97:11). The verse closes the Jewish Havdalah, the short service at the end of the Sabbath, where the family adds "so may it be for us." The Talmud reads its four nouns as four commandments that Haman had tried to stop: "light" is the Torah, "joy" is the festivals, "gladness" is circumcision, and "honor" is tefillin (Bavli Megillah 16b). The plain sense is the reverse of 4:3, where "the Jews mourned deeply. They fasted, wept and cried aloud."

a: made themselves Jews
p: The verb mityahadim appears only here. It may mean they converted, claimed to be Jews, or took the Jews' side.
b: The verb is formed from the word "Jew" with a reflexive ending, literally "made themselves Jews." Three readings: (1) they converted: the Greek says they "were circumcised and lived as Jews" (see the variant); (2) they pretended to be Jews, to be safe, a view held by some traditional and modern commentators; Josephus stands between the two, saying that many of the nations "had themselves circumcised out of fear of the Jews," to make themselves safe (Antiquities 11.285); (3) they sided with the Jews, as the officials do in 9:3. "Dread" points to safety more than faith, though the Bible often treats fear of God's people as the start of turning to him (Joshua 2:9–11). Either way the verse looks ahead to 9:27, which speaks of "everyone who would join them."

a: since dread of the Jews had come down on them
p: The language recalls the dread that fell on Canaan before Israel in the Exodus and conquest stories.
b: The Hebrew says dread "fell" on them (nafal pachad), as in the Song at the Sea, "Terror and dread fall on them" (Exodus 15:16), and Rahab's words, "Dread of you has fallen on us" (Joshua 2:9). Deuteronomy promised that God would put "the dread and fear of you on the peoples everywhere under the sky" (Deuteronomy 2:25). The same phrase comes twice more in 9:2–3. God is not named, but the language belongs to the old stories of God fighting for Israel, which is why many readers see his hand here.

a: But it was turned upside down.
p: Two Hebrew words, venahafokh hu, sum up the whole book: everything is reversed.
b: Venahafokh hu means "and it was overturned." The verb hafakh is used of Sodom's overthrow (Genesis 19:25) and of mourning turned to dancing (Psalm 30:11); in 9:22 the month is "changed" (nehpakh) from grief to joy. Scholars list the book's reversals: Haman plans Mordecai's honor and gets it for him (6); Haman hangs on his own pole (7:10); Mordecai gets Haman's ring and house (8:2); a decree of death becomes a decree of defense (8:11); the city in turmoil cheers (3:15; 8:15). Purim customs that turn things upside down, costumes and plays, grow from this verse. The text does not say who turned it, and leaves the reader to ask. The Septuagint lacks these words: its 9:1 says only that "the letters written by the king arrived" (see the variant).

a: were backing the Jews
p: The empire's officials help the Jews, because Mordecai now holds the king's power.
b: The officials who received Haman's letters (3:12) now "lift up" (menasse'im) the Jews, as officials "supported" Ezra's people with gifts (Ezra 1:4; Ezra 8:36). The narrator gives a realistic reason: "dread of Mordecai," the new holder of the king's ring. In a Persian province, two royal decrees were in force at once; officials naturally backed the one whose author stood next to the king. The story thus shows ordinary politics bringing about the rescue.

a: as the man Mordecai kept on growing greater
p: The Hebrew uses the same words as 2 Samuel 5:10: "David kept on growing greater."
b: The phrase holekh vegadol, "going and growing great," is used of David: "David kept on growing greater, and the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him" (2 Samuel 5:10; compare 2 Samuel 3:1 and 1 Samuel 2:26). Mordecai's rise thus echoes David's rise over the house of Saul. In Samuel the second half of the sentence names the LORD; Esther keeps only the first half. Many readers think the silence is deliberate, and that the reader is meant to finish the sentence.

a: They treated those who hated them however they wanted
p: The killing in chapter 9 troubles many readers. Jewish, Christian and critical readers have answered in different ways.
b: Self-defense under an unchangeable law. The king could not undo Haman's decree (8:8); the Jews strike only on the day fixed for their own destruction, against "anyone who was looking to do them harm" (9:2), and take no plunder (9:10, 15, 16). So Baldwin, Bush and Berlin, among many. Revenge. Paton wrote that the book has not one noble character, and Luther wished it did not exist, because, he said, it and 2 Maccabees "Judaize too much" (Table Talk) (a complaint about its Jewishness as much as its violence). The Jewish historian Elliott Horowitz has traced how the memory of Purim was linked to violence, down to the massacre at the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron on Purim 1994 (Horowitz). A story of reversal. Many scholars read the numbers as part of a tale where every threat is paid back in kind, to give hope to a people at others' mercy (Fox, Levenson, Clines). The Greek lacks this verse (see the variant).

a: the Jews killed five hundred men
p: The text counts "men" (ish) in Susa, both on the 13th and on the 14th.
b: The number five hundred is given as "five hundred man," the singular ish as often with numbers. The same word is used in 9:12 and 9:15 (three hundred men). Readers who take 8:11 as permission to kill women and children note that the narrator never reports that it happened; the counts are of men. The fighting takes place "in the fortress at Susa," the royal quarter itself, where Haman's household and allies lived.

a: And they killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
t: The ten sons in a column
p: Scrolls write the ten names in a column, read in one breath. A modern claim links small letters here to 1946.
b: The names are Persian in form, though their meanings are uncertain. Jewish scrolls write them in a special layout: each name on its own line on the right, with the word ve'et (the object marker) on the left, like bricks stacked without overlap (Bavli Megillah 16b). The reader says all ten in one breath, which the Talmud explains as "their souls went out together." Some scrolls write the taw of Parshandatha, the shin of Parmashta and the zayin of Vaizatha small, and the waw of Vaizatha large. In the 20th century people noticed that these letters can spell the Jewish year 5707, which is 1946, when ten Nazi leaders were hanged at Nuremberg, and that Julius Streicher shouted "Purim festival 1946" on the scaffold. The Streicher detail was reported at the time; the letters themselves are a medieval scribal custom with no known link to such a reading.

a: But they kept their hands off the plunder.
p: Said three times. Saul took Amalek's spoil and lost his kingdom; Mordecai's people refuse it.
b: The decree allowed plunder (8:11), as Haman's had (3:13), but the Jews would not "stretch out a hand" to it. Many see a deliberate contrast with 1 Samuel 15. Saul, son of Kish the Benjaminite (1 Samuel 9:1–2), was told to put Amalek under the ban, but he "and the people took pity on Agag, and on the pick of the sheep and cattle" (1 Samuel 15:9), and Samuel asked, "Why did you swoop down on the spoil and do what is evil in the LORD's eyes?" (1 Samuel 15:19). Mordecai is "the son of Kish, a man of Benjamin" (2:5), and Haman is "the Agagite" (3:1). This time the Benjaminite's people kill Agag's heirs and touch nothing. Abraham's refusal of the spoils of Sodom may also be in the background (Genesis 14:22–23). The Greek reads "and they plundered" (see the variant).

a: let the Jews in Susa be given tomorrow as well
t: Esther's request for a second day
p: Esther asks for a second day in Susa: vindictive, prudent, or the origin of a second feast day?
b: Vindictive. Paton and other older critics saw her request as bloodthirsty, and it has often been cited against the book's morality. Prudent. Others argue that enemies remained in the capital and that Esther knew more than the king's count showed; the decree allowed only one day (8:12), so another was needed to end the danger (Baldwin, Jobes, Bush). Explaining the calendar. Many critical scholars think the scene exists to explain why Susa, and later walled cities, keep Purim on the 15th of Adar while others keep the 14th (9:18–19; Clines, Fox). The Hebrew gives no motive. The Greek versions do: the Septuagint asks for the second day "so as to hang the ten sons of Haman," making the display the purpose, and the Alpha Text has Esther ask that the Jews may "destroy and plunder" whomever they wish, a harsher request that reverses the Hebrew's refusal of plunder (see the variant).

a: let Haman's ten sons be hung on the pole
p: The sons were killed in 9:7–10. Hanging their bodies put them on public display, a known ancient practice.
b: The Plain uses "hung" for putting bodies on display (9:13–14, 25) and "hanged" for an execution (7:10). Displaying the bodies of executed enemies was common: the Philistines hung Saul's body on the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10), and Joshua hung the bodies of the five kings on trees until evening (Joshua 10:26). Deuteronomy limits the practice, "his body must not stay on the tree overnight" (Deuteronomy 21:23). The Greek of 9:14 says the king "set out" the bodies of Haman's sons, which also suggests display. Haman's whole house thus shares his fate on the same pole (9:25).

a: They had rest from their enemies.
p: Deuteronomy ties "rest from all your enemies" to the command to wipe out Amalek's memory.
b: The verb nuach, "rest," runs through these verses (9:16, 17, 18, 22) and names what the feast celebrates: not victory, but rest. Deuteronomy uses the same words in the command about Amalek: "The LORD your God will give you rest from all your enemies around you... When he does, wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky" (Deuteronomy 25:19). Since Haman is Agag's heir (3:1), many readers think the link is intended. The same "rest" came to Israel in Joshua's day (Joshua 21:44) and in David's (2 Samuel 7:1).

a: seventy-five thousand
p: The Greek has 15,000. Critics see a storyteller's number; others think it plausible across 127 provinces.
b: The figure covers the whole empire on a single day. Readers who take the book as history note that it is spread over 127 provinces and that the Jews fought only those who attacked them (Baldwin, Jobes). Many critical scholars see it as one of the book's large, rounded numbers, like the 180-day feast (1:4) and the ten thousand talents (3:9), suited to a story of reversal rather than an exact count (Fox, Clines). The Septuagint has fifteen thousand (see the variant). No outside source mentions the event.

a: the village Jews, who live in the towns of the open country
p: Villagers kept the 14th of Adar, Susa the 15th. The Mishnah turned this into a rule about walled cities.
b: Perazim are open, unwalled settlements (Deuteronomy 3:5; Ezekiel 38:11); the written form of the word in this verse differs slightly from the spoken one. The verse explains a custom already in force in the writer's day. The Mishnah fixed it as law: towns walled since Joshua's day read the Megillah on the 15th, "Shushan Purim," and other places on the 14th (Mishnah Megillah 1:1). Today Jerusalem keeps the 15th. The Greek adds that city dwellers keep the 15th (see the variant).

a: a day for sending portions of food to one another
p: The same custom appears in Nehemiah 8. Jews still send mishloach manot on Purim.
b: Mishloach manot, "sending of portions," is how Purim is still kept: plates of ready-to-eat food sent to friends. Nehemiah uses the same word manot when the leaders tell the people to "send shares to those who have nothing ready" (Nehemiah 8:10), and the people go "to send out shares and to make great joy" (Nehemiah 8:12). In both books a holy day of joy is marked by food shared with others. Mordecai's letter adds gifts to the poor (9:22).

a: Mordecai wrote these things down
p: The style turns legal here. Many think 9:20–32 was added; others read it as the story's goal.
b: "These things" may mean the events just told, or the whole book: some traditional readers took the verse to say that Mordecai wrote the book of Esther, while the Talmud credits the men of the Great Assembly (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). The Septuagint says he wrote these words "in a book." The section has its own vocabulary of binding and confirming (qiyyem, "make binding," 9:21, 27, 29, 31, 32), retells the plot briefly with some differences (9:24–25), and is mostly missing from the Greek Alpha Text. Paton, Clines and others think it was added to fix a festival already being kept; Fox and Levenson stress that the story was always meant to end in a festival. Traditional readers see Mordecai and Esther writing to bind a festival on all the Jews.

a: year after year
p: 1 Maccabees tells how Hanukkah and Nicanor's Day were set up by decree, as Mordecai set up Purim.
b: Purim is a feast the law of Moses never commands. Mordecai's letter made it a duty, and the Jews took it on themselves (9:27). 1 Maccabees tells of two later feasts set up the same way. When the temple altar was made new in 164 BC, Judas, his brothers and the people "decided that the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept at their season every year, for eight days" (1 Maccabees 4:59). This is Hanukkah. After Judas beat the Syrian general Nicanor in 161 BC, "They resolved to keep this day every year, on the thirteenth of Adar" (1 Maccabees 7:49). That was the day before Purim, "one day before Mordecai's Day," as 2 Maccabees 15:36 says. Like Purim, these feasts rest on a decree of the people, not on a command in the Torah.

a: from grief to joy and from mourning to a holiday
p: The prophets promised that mourning would be turned to joy. Esther tells it happening in a foreign land.
b: Jeremiah promises a scattered Israel, "I will change their mourning into joy" (Jeremiah 31:13), and a psalm thanks God, "My mourning song you changed into a dance for me" (Psalm 30:11). Zechariah says the fasts of the exile will become "joy and gladness and good feasts" for Judah (Zechariah 8:19). Jesus tells his disciples that their grief will turn to joy (John 16:20). Esther's month of Adar, "changed" (nehpakh, the same verb as 9:1) from grief to joy, is that promise kept for Jews still in exile, without a prophet to announce it. These prophetic books are not yet translated on this site.

a: presents to the needy
p: Purim requires gifts to at least two poor people. Maimonides said to give the poor more than you spend on the feast.
b: Mattanot la'evyonim, "gifts to the needy," is one of the four commandments of Purim, with hearing the Megillah, the feast, and sending portions. The Talmud rules that each person gives to at least two poor people (Bavli Megillah 7a). Maimonides wrote that it is better to give more gifts to the poor than to make one's feast or one's gifts to friends more lavish, "for there is no greater and more splendid joy than to gladden the hearts of the poor, orphans, widows and strangers" (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Megillah 2:17). A feast of rescue becomes a feast that rescues others.

a: He had cast Pur, that is, the lot
p: Mordecai's letter retells 3:7. "Throw into panic" is the word for the panic God sends on Israel's enemies.
b: On pur, the Akkadian word for a lot, and the inscribed Assyrian die that calls itself a puru, see the note on 3:7. Mordecai's letter adds a detail the story did not give: Haman cast the lot "to rout them in panic" (lehummam), a word that sounds like Haman's own name, a play most commentators notice. Hamam is the verb for the confusion God throws on Israel's enemies in battle (Exodus 14:24; Joshua 10:10; Judges 4:15; 1 Samuel 7:10). Haman tried to do to the Jews what God does to his enemies. The lot was meant to pick a day of doom; its name became the name of the Jews' feast (9:26). The Greek has "he made a decree and a lot" and calls Haman "the Macedonian" (see the variant).
orig: לְהֻמָּם וּלְאַבְּדָם (lehummam ul'abbedam), 'to rout them in panic and to destroy them'

a: But when the matter came before the king
t: When she came, or when it came?
p: The Hebrew "when it came" is feminine and may mean Esther. The summary also differs from chapters 5–7.
b: Uvo'ah is "and when she/it came." It may refer to Esther (KJV supplies "Esther," and Rashi reads it so), or to Haman's plot (the feminine noun machashavto in 9:24). The summary that follows is shorter and different from the story: Esther's feasts are not mentioned, the king gives orders "in writing," and Haman and his sons are hanged together, though the sons died months later (9:10–14). The Septuagint makes the subject Haman: "how he went in to the king, saying to hang Mordecai" (see the variant). Critical scholars take the differences as a sign that 9:20–32 comes from a separate source (Clines); others read it as a legal summary that compresses events (Fox).

a: So these days were named Purim, from the name Pur.
p: The book derives the name from Haman's lot. Scholars once tied Purim to a Babylonian or Persian feast.
b: The book's account: the feast commemorates the rescue, and its plural name, "Lots," recalls Haman's lot (3:7; 9:24). In 1891–92, Heinrich Zimmern and Peter Jensen argued that the story was a Jewish version of a Babylonian myth: Mordecai = Marduk, Esther = Ishtar, Haman = the Elamite god Humban, Vashti = an Elamite goddess, with Purim from the Babylonian New Year, when the gods fixed fates. Paul de Lagarde (1887) proposed the Persian feast of the dead, Farvardigan, and Theodor Gaster (1950) an adaptation of the Persian New Year. Verdict: the name links are real (Mordecai's name is built on Marduk, as Jews in exile often bore such names; compare Daniel 1:7), but no myth with this plot is known, and most scholars now see Purim as a Jewish diaspora festival whose story is its founding account, whatever older customs it absorbed (Moore, Fox). The first outside mention is "Mordecai's day" in 2 Maccabees 15:36.

a: took it on as binding
p: The Talmud reads this verse to say that in Esther's day the Jews took the Torah on themselves again, this time freely.
b: The words are qiyyemu veqibbelu, "they established and accepted." The written text has qibbel, "he accepted" (singular, treating the Jews as one), and the reading tradition has the plural. The Talmud says that at Sinai Israel accepted the Torah under pressure, but "they upheld and accepted" means that in Ahasuerus' day they upheld out of love what they had accepted long before (Bavli Shabbat 88a). The plain sense is that the Jews bound themselves to keep Purim, a festival not commanded in the law of Moses, and so the verse became a key text for how later Judaism could add binding customs.
orig: קִיְּמוּ וְקִבְּלֻ (qiyyemu veqibbelu; written וְקִבֵּל, veqibbel)

a: for everyone who would join them
p: The word nilvim is used of foreigners who join themselves to the LORD (Isaiah 56:3, 6).
b: The participle hannilvim, "those joining," is the word Isaiah uses: "Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say..." (Isaiah 56:3, 6; compare Zechariah 2:11). Here it points back to the "many people from the peoples of the land" who "made themselves Jews" (8:17). Purim binds converts as well as those born Jewish. The book that began with a decree against "a certain people" (3:8) ends with that people open to newcomers.

a: These days were to be remembered
p: On the Sabbath before Purim, synagogues read Deuteronomy's command to remember Amalek.
b: The verb zakhar, "remember," links Purim to the Amalek command: "Remember what Amalek did to you on the road when you came out of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 25:17), and "Write this down in the scroll as a reminder" (Exodus 17:14). The Sabbath before Purim is called Shabbat Zakhor, "the Sabbath of Remember," when Deuteronomy 25:17–19 is read (Mishnah Megillah 3:4), and on Purim morning the Torah reading is Exodus 17:8–16. Noisemakers drown out Haman's name in the Megillah reading, a playful way of blotting out the memory of Amalek.

a: Queen Esther, Abihail's daughter, wrote with Mordecai the Jew
p: "Wrote" is feminine singular. Esther writes with authority; the Talmud says she asked to be written down.
b: The Hebrew vattikhtov, "and she wrote," puts Esther first, with Mordecai added; 9:30 then says "he sent." It is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where a woman writes a binding religious ruling for all Israel. "This second letter" may mean that hers confirms Mordecai's first one (9:20), or "second" may be a later note: the Septuagint has no such word, reading only "the confirmation of the letter of Phrourai," and some commentators delete it (Moore; see the variant). The Talmud tells that Esther asked the sages to "write me down for the generations," and they at first refused (Bavli Megillah 7a), a story about the book's fight for a place in the canon. The Greek calls her father Aminadab (see the variant).

a: with words of peace and truth
p: The same pair closes Zechariah's promise that fasts will become feasts: "love truth and peace" (Zechariah 8:19).
b: Zechariah was asked whether the exile fasts should go on. His answer: the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months "will become joy and gladness and good feasts for the house of Judah," so "love truth and peace" (Zechariah 8:19). Esther's letter speaks of fasts (9:31) and of a feast, and uses the same two words, shalom ve'emet, "peace and truth." Many think the writer knew the passage (Berlin). The Septuagint lacks this verse, so the echo is a feature of the Hebrew only (see the variant). "Peace" may also be the standard greeting of a letter (compare Ezra 4:17; Daniel 4:1).

a: the rules about the fasts and their cries for help
t: Fasts and the Fast of Esther
p: The fasts recall chapter 4. This verse is why Purim's feast has a fast before it.
b: "The fasts and their cries" look back to 4:3, where the Jews "fasted, wept and cried aloud," and to Esther's three-day fast (4:16). The verse says the Jews had already taken these on themselves, so Purim is set within a pattern of fasting followed by feasting. The Fast of Esther, kept on the 13th of Adar, the day of the fighting, takes its basis from this verse (see the note on 4:16). It is not mentioned in the Talmud; its first clear witnesses are the eighth-century She'iltot of Rav Achai and the tractate Soferim. The Septuagint of 9:31 has no fasts at all (see the variant), so the custom rests on the Hebrew alone. Some scholars think the verse refers to fasts the Jews already kept, such as those named in Zechariah 8:19.

a: and it was written in the book
p: The "book" may be the royal records, a Jewish record of Purim, or the scroll of Esther itself.
b: The Hebrew says simply "in the book" (bassefer). (1) The royal records named in 2:23, 6:1 and 10:2. (2) A Jewish record of Purim rules, now lost. The Septuagint reads "it was written as a memorial" instead (see the variant). (3) This very book: Jewish tradition reads the verse with Esther's request to be written down (Bavli Megillah 7a). The question connects to Esther's long road into the canon. Some rabbis said it does not "make the hands unclean," that is, is not holy Scripture (Bavli Megillah 7a, Rabbi Samuel's view), though it was read in public. No copy has been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Athanasius of Alexandria listed it among books to be read but not in the canon (Festal Letter 39). Jews and most Christians now count it fully as Scripture.

a: King Ahasuerus put a tax on the land and on the islands of the sea
t: A tax on land and islands
p: The word mas usually means forced labor or tribute. After 479 BC Persia lost most of the Aegean islands.
b: Mas is the word for Solomon's forced labor (1 Kings 5:13; 9:21); later it came to mean tribute or tax. "The islands of the sea" (or "coastlands") means the far western edge of the empire. Herodotus lists the tribute Darius set for each province (Herodotus, Histories 3.89–97). After Xerxes' defeat by the Greeks in 480–479 BC, Persia lost control of most of the Aegean islands, so the verse may describe royal claims more than real income, or reflect a writer far from the scene. Why the book ends with taxes is debated: as a sign of the king's continuing power, or of a stable empire in which a Jew now holds second place. The written text spells the king's name Achashresh here, a shorter form.

a: are written in the book of the daily records of the kings of Media and Persia, are they not?
t: Like the end of a king's reign
p: The book closes with the formula of Kings: "Is it not written in the records?"
b: Kings ends each reign this way: "The rest of Nadab's story, and all he did, is written in the scroll of the records of the kings of Israel, is it not?" (1 Kings 15:31; compare 1 Kings 11:41). Esther uses the same formula for a Persian king and his Jewish second-in-command, so Mordecai's greatness is set in an official record. No Persian royal chronicle of this kind has survived. Note the order "Media and Persia," as in Daniel 8:20, though elsewhere Esther says "Persia and Media" (1:3, 14, 18, 19).

a: next in rank after King Ahasuerus
p: Like Joseph and Daniel, Mordecai ends second in the empire, "welcomed by the crowd of his brothers."
b: Mishneh lammelekh, "second to the king," recalls Joseph in Pharaoh's "second chariot" (Genesis 41:43) and Daniel raised to high office in Babylon and Persia (Daniel 5:29; Daniel 6:2–3); 2 Chronicles 28:7 uses the same title for an officer of Judah's king. The Talmud notices that Mordecai was welcomed by "the crowd" (rov, "the majority") of his brothers, not all of them, and says some sages kept their distance because he left the study of Torah for public office (Bavli Megillah 16b). On the Persian tablets naming officials called Marduka, see the note on 2:5. Greek sources name no Jewish second-in-command under Xerxes.

a: spoke peace to all his offspring
p: The Hebrew says "his seed." It may mean his descendants, or, as many take it, his whole race.
b: Zar'o, "his seed," usually means descendants, and some take it so: Mordecai's peace was for his family after him. But it stands in parallel with "his people" and may mean the Jewish people as a whole, as "the seed of the Jews" does in 6:13 (Fox; BSB "countrymen"); in 9:27–28 the same word means descendants. "Speaking peace" means working for their welfare (compare Psalm 85:8; Zechariah 9:10). The Hebrew book ends here, with no word of God and no word of return to the land, but with a Jew in high office caring for his people. The Greek goes on with Addition F and a note on the translation (see the variant).
orig: וְדֹבֵר שָׁלוֹם לְכָל־זַרְעוֹ (vedover shalom lekhol zar'o)
